title: West Sikkim permits and practical tips for 2025–26
meta_description: West and South Sikkim practical guide: permits for Indians and foreigners, ATMs, mobile network, plastic rules, monsoon roads, drive times and shared jeeps.
summary: Indians need no permit for Pelling, Yuksom, Ravangla or Namchi; foreigners need a free Sikkim Restricted Area Permit, and Goecha La or Dzongri need park permits and a guide. Carry cash, because village ATMs and network are thin. Avoid travel after dark, allow for landslides in the monsoon, and respect Sikkim's strict plastic rules.

sections.heading: Permits for Indians and foreigners
paras: For Indian citizens, West and South Sikkim are open. You need no permit for Pelling, Yuksom, Khecheopalri, Tashiding, Rinchenpong, Uttarey, Ravangla, Namchi or Temi. Carry a government photo ID, because hotels must record it and police at checkposts such as Melli or Rangpo may ask to see it. Children should carry a school ID or birth certificate copy.

Foreign nationals need a Sikkim Restricted Area Permit, usually called the RAP. It is free and is normally issued online as an e-RAP or at entry points such as the Rangpo and Melli checkposts, as well as through Sikkim Tourism offices and Indian missions abroad. It is usually issued for 30 days. You need your passport, Indian visa and photos. Bhutanese citizens do not need it. These rules have changed before; check current status before you travel.

Indian travellers coming from Darjeeling or Kalimpong can cross into Sikkim at Jorethang, Melli or Rangpo without any paperwork beyond ID. Foreign travellers on that same route must carry the RAP before reaching the checkpost, or arrange it at the checkpost itself where that service is running. Note that the RAP for West and South Sikkim does not cover protected areas in the north and east, which need separate permits through an agency.
list: Keep several photocopies of your ID, passport and permit; checkposts and hotels may each want one.
If you cross from Darjeeling via Jorethang, foreigners must have the RAP stamped or verified at the checkpost; do not skip it.
Uttarey sits close to the Nepal border. Walking over Chewabhanjyang into Nepal is not an official crossing for tourists.

sections.heading: Goecha La, Dzongri and park permits
paras: Treks into Khangchendzonga National Park need a park entry permit from the forest office at Yuksom and a licensed guide. Indians register there with photo ID; foreigners also need a trekking permit through a registered Sikkim travel agency, normally for a group of two or more. Day walks around Yuksom, to Dubdi and to Tashi Tenka, need nothing. Barsey Rhododendron Sanctuary and Maenam Wildlife Sanctuary charge small entry fees at the gate, usually under ₹100 for Indians and more for foreigners. In recent seasons Goecha La treks have been allowed only to View Point 1. Check current status before you travel.

sections.heading: Cash, ATMs and mobile network
paras: Carry more cash than you think you need. ATMs exist in the district towns, Gyalshing, Jorethang, Namchi and Ravangla, and there are one or two in Pelling, but they run out of notes on long weekends and in festival weeks. In villages such as Uttarey, Hee Bermiok, Okhrey and Khecheopalri there is no ATM at all. UPI is widely accepted, from homestays to jeep counters, but only works when the phone signal does.

Jio and Airtel give usable 4G in Pelling, Gyalshing, Jorethang, Namchi and Ravangla, with BSNL often the only signal in the higher villages. Coverage fades on the Yuksom road and is weak to absent on treks beyond Tshoka and in parts of Barsey. Download offline maps and tell your homestay your arrival time before you lose signal.
list: Keep ₹3,000–5,000 in small notes per person for jeep fares, tea stalls, entry fees and homestays that cannot take UPI.
Power cuts are common in the monsoon; carry a power bank and a small torch.
SIM cards from other Indian states roam normally; foreign travellers usually buy a local prepaid SIM in Siliguri with passport and visa copies before coming up.

sections.heading: Roads, landslides and drive times
paras: Sikkim's hill roads average 20–30 km an hour, slower in rain or road works, so plan your days by hours rather than kilometres. From June to September monsoon landslides can block a road for an hour or several days. The Teesta valley road, NH10, which many drivers use to reach Melli and Jorethang, has had long closures and diversions since the October 2023 Teesta flood. Drivers sometimes reroute via Darjeeling or Kalimpong. Check current status before you travel and always keep one spare day before a train or flight.
list: A reserved small car from NJP to Pelling costs about ₹5,000–6,500, and to Ravangla about ₹4,500–5,500.
Do not drive or ride after dark: roads are unlit, edges are soft and drivers stop for good reason.

sections.heading: Shared jeeps: how they work
paras: Shared jeeps are the backbone of travel here, cheap and frequent on the main routes and rare on village roads. Most leave from a stand or counter in each town, such as the SNT and jeep stands in Siliguri, the Jorethang stand and the Gyalshing taxi stand, and most long-distance jeeps leave between 6 and 11 am.
list: Buy your seat at the counter, ideally the evening before; the ticket usually carries a seat number.
Front seats go first. If you get carsick, ask for a front or window seat when you book.
Luggage rides on the roof under a tarpaulin. Pack valuables, medicines and a jacket in a day bag you keep with you.
Jeeps leave when full. If you are short of time, you can buy the empty seats to go sooner.
No smoking inside. Drivers stop for tea and toilets about once every two hours.
Be at the stand 15 minutes early; a jeep will not wait long for one late passenger.

sections.heading: Seasons, health and what to pack
paras: The clearest months are October to December and March to April, when Kanchenjunga shows at dawn from Pelling, Rinchenpong and Ravangla. Days are pleasant at 12–20 °C in the towns, but nights drop to 2–8 °C in winter, and colder in Uttarey or Okhrey. May is warm and hazy, and June to September is wet. Pharmacies exist in Gyalshing, Pelling, Jorethang, Namchi and Ravangla, and district hospitals are in Gyalshing and Namchi, but villages have only small health centres, so carry what you need.
list: A warm layer and a rain jacket in every season; mornings are cold even in May.
Walking shoes with grip for wet stone steps at Dubdi, Sanga Choeling and Tashiding.
Your own medicines, motion-sickness tablets for the hill roads, oral rehydration salts and a basic first-aid kit.
A refillable bottle, a cloth bag and a small bag to carry your rubbish back to town.
Sunscreen and sunglasses: the sun at 2,000 m and above burns faster than on the plains.
Travel insurance, and for treks, cover for walking up to 5,000 m.

sections.heading: Plastic, altitude, safety and dress
paras: Sikkim has some of India's strictest plastic rules. Polythene carry bags have been banned for decades, single-use plastics and styrofoam plates are restricted, and packaged drinking water bottles are banned or discouraged in a growing list of places. Some villages and sanctuaries also charge a small green or entry fee. Carry a refillable bottle and a cloth bag, refill from filtered water at homestays and hotels, and take your wrappers back to town. Check current status before you travel, because local rules change.

West Sikkim's towns sit between about 1,500 and 2,200 m, which most people feel only as cold mornings. Altitude becomes a real concern on the Dzongri and Goecha La treks, at Barsey above 3,000 m and on the Maenam hike. Climb slowly, drink water and come down if a headache gets worse.
list: Crime against travellers is rare. The real risks are roads, weather, wet rocks and rivers: never swim in the Rangeet or Teesta.
At monasteries cover shoulders and knees, take off shoes and hats, walk clockwise and ask before photographing inside.
Leeches are common on forest paths from June to September; salt and long socks help.
Save the police control room and your homestay's number on paper as well as on your phone.

faqs.q: Do Indians need a permit to visit Pelling and Yuksom?
faqs.a: No. Indian citizens need no permit for Pelling, Yuksom, Khecheopalri, Rinchenpong, Ravangla, Namchi or anywhere else in West and South Sikkim. Carry a government photo ID, because hotels record it and checkposts may ask. A permit is needed only for treks into Khangchendzonga National Park, such as Dzongri and Goecha La, which also require a licensed guide.

faqs.q: How do foreigners get a Sikkim permit?
faqs.a: Foreign nationals need a free Sikkim Restricted Area Permit, usually issued online as an e-RAP or at entry checkposts such as Rangpo and Melli, and through Sikkim Tourism offices. You need your passport, Indian visa and photos, and it is usually valid for 30 days. Keep copies, because hotels and checkposts ask. Check current status before you travel.

faqs.q: Are there ATMs in Pelling and Yuksom?
faqs.a: Pelling has one or two ATMs and Gyalshing, about 10 km below, has more, but they can run dry on long weekends. Do not rely on finding a working ATM in Yuksom or in villages such as Uttarey, Hee Bermiok or Okhrey. Draw cash in Siliguri, Jorethang or Gyalshing and carry ₹3,000–5,000 per person in small notes.

faqs.q: Which mobile network works best in West Sikkim?
faqs.a: Jio and Airtel work well in Pelling, Gyalshing, Jorethang, Namchi and Ravangla. BSNL is often the only signal in higher villages and on some ridges. On the Yuksom road, around Barsey and on the Goecha La trail, expect long gaps with no signal at all. Download offline maps and share your plans before you leave town.

faqs.q: Is it safe to travel to West Sikkim in the monsoon?
faqs.a: It is possible but slow and sometimes disrupted. From June to September landslides can block roads for hours or days, views are mostly in cloud and treks are best avoided. The Teesta road has had long closures since the October 2023 flood. If you go, keep spare days, travel only in daylight and check current status before you travel.

faqs.q: How long does it take from Siliguri to Pelling?
faqs.a: About 5–6 hours for roughly 135 km, via Sevoke, Melli and Jorethang or Gyalshing. A few direct shared jeeps leave Siliguri in the morning for ₹450–600 a seat; otherwise go to Jorethang for ₹250–350 and change. A reserved small car from NJP costs about ₹5,000–6,500. Road works and landslides can add hours.

faqs.q: Are plastic bottles banned in Sikkim?
faqs.a: Sikkim restricts plastic more strictly than most states: polythene bags have long been banned, single-use plastics are curbed, and packaged drinking water bottles are banned or discouraged in a growing list of places. Rules and enforcement vary by area, so carry a refillable bottle, refill from filtered water at your stay and check current status before you travel.

faqs.q: How do shared jeeps work in Sikkim?
faqs.a: You buy a numbered seat at the counter of a jeep stand, ideally the evening before, and the jeep leaves when it is full, mostly in the morning. Luggage goes on the roof under a tarpaulin. Fares are fixed per seat, for example ₹150–220 from Jorethang to Pelling. If you are in a hurry you can buy the empty seats.

faqs.q: What should I wear when visiting monasteries in Sikkim?
faqs.a: Clothes that cover shoulders and knees, with shoes you can take off quickly at the prayer-hall door. Remove hats inside, walk clockwise around chortens and prayer wheels, and ask before taking photos, which are often banned inside. A light shawl or jacket is useful anyway, because mornings at 2,000 m are cool even in spring.
